chapters.html:
Mydei!

What, too busy doing whatever it is Princes do to spar with me?

Oh? You're helping this girl here find her doll? Well, surely you'll need the Deliverer’s help for a task as important as that!

~

Mydei wakes with a start, still unused to the air in Ohkema. The fuzz in his head that has been there since he arrived certainly has not helped. The root cause, he considers as he rolls out of bed– he's a bit stiff, he notices, he should have gone to the baths last night– is the dreams he's been having.

Everyone in Amphoreus knows of the Deliverer. They are the one who everybody is waiting for, who the prophecy declared would save them all.

However– Mydei has asked around, subtly, and only he dreams of him. It's annoying not having an explanation, but a part of him likes having him in his brilliance all to himself.

~

The Kremnoan dictionary must be very short indeed. Tell me– do you even have a word for fun?

No? Oh, Mydei, how you wound me! For what are we having right now?

What do you mean, “at my expense”?

~

Cyrene is away, and has been for some time. He wishes he could ask her about the Deliverer to at least learn his name. She seems to be the one who knows him best, if all the stories are true, and so might just be able to answer his questions.

Because– Mydei isn't interested in tales of their bravery and heroic fate. The only thing he really wants to know is why he went out of his way to play with Ohkema’s orphaned children, and why he smiled when he ate Mydei's food even if he made it bland on purpose, and why he looked– so sad, all the time, like he'd lost hope for his own future and was only fighting on for the sake of everyone else.

He can guess, but he wants to know more. He wishes he could ask the Deliverer directly, but it doesn't seem like he'll get the chance.

~

Crown Prince of Castrum Kremnos, I challenge you to a duel.

A Kremnos Festival, you say? Sounds perfect.

Don't expect that you'll win– and please, don't go easy on me just because I can die. A victory like that is no victory at all.

~

“Do you think the Deliverer will come back?” He asks, his knee bouncing despite himself.

“They have to,” says Hyacine, stitching up his shoulder. He'd gotten a bit injured in a recent bout with some monster, but it's nothing she can't heal.

Still, he probably should take someone with him to watch his back, but he doesn't feel like there's anyone strong enough to keep up with him when he fights. It should be fine on his own, if unpleasant.

“I dream about him,” Mydei admits. It's not really a secret, he's mentioned it before, but it's not something he talks about too often. His dreams feel intimate, private. “He's got– white hair, and a greatsword, and these blue eyes–”

“Mydei,” Hyacine says carefully, setting down her needle, “the Deliverer is a girl.”

“What?”

He combs back through his memories, and finds he cannot doubt them. This, this, is the Deliverer. This is who Mydei believes in and who he has been waiting for his whole life.

“Her name is Stelle,” Hyacine says in soothing tones only a nurse can manage. “She's got grey hair, and wields a bat.”

He tries to consider that for a moment, and frowns. It's not that he dislikes this De– Stelle, he somehow gets the feeling that he'd approve of her, but to him the true Deliverer has always been and will always be that white-haired boy. Mydei feels like he knew him even before he started dreaming of him, no matter how impossible that sounds.

“The one I know…” he starts, but he isn't sure how to put into words what's so special about the boy in his head.

“I think you ought to talk to Cyrene,” Hyacine tells him. It sounds like a Doctor's order. “She's supposed to come back next week.”

~

Come on. Think of the Era Nova.

You know, sometimes I almost feel like I can just reach out and grab it.

Don't get too reckless, Mydei. I want you there with me.

Of course I do! What, don't tell me you didn't know?

You really didn't? Well, I'll put it plainly. Mydeimos, I–

~

“You're Cyrene?”

“Yes,” says the pink-haired girl in the garden. She looks at him like he is an old friend. If she has all the memories of the Heirs from a previous life, like he's been told, then he supposes he really is one.

“I've been having dreams,” he says bluntly.

“Dreams are a kind of memory,” Cyrene answers, getting at his question through his wording. “They tend to reveal things that are, at least in a way, true.”

“The Deliverer,” he asks, “what are they like?”

“She's determined,” Cyrene says, and Mydei feels his heart sink a touch. “I believe she's going to save us.”

“I don't mean her.”

Cyrene laughs, and it's a little sad.

“I see. You mean the other Deliverer.”

She signs, and gazes off towards Kephale for a moment. Mydei recalls that Stelle is supposed to inherit the Worldbearing Coreflame. Then– his Deliverer–

“He and I were friends, a long time ago, but you ended up knowing him better than I ever did.”

“So he's real?”

“The fate of your Deliverer is so tragic that he warps the world around him to that genre,” she says. “This loop is much kinder than the one he lived in, though only because of his sacrifice.”

“Is he–” Mydei starts, and then stops, because he isn't really sure what he wants to say. There's so much he wants to ask to such an extent that he's paralyzed.

“He's alive,” Cyrene confirms. “As far as I know, he's still fighting Irontomb. His signal went dark, but there's no evidence it was terminated.”

He tries to imagine the boy of his dreams fighting a god made to kill gods of thousands of years. The image doesn't sit right. The Deliverer, he's sure, is far more gentle than his tenacity forces him to be.

“What's his name?” He asks.

“Khaslana,” Cyrene responds. “But for you and I? Phainon, of Aedes Elysiae.”

~

You should have seen the wheat fields, Mydei. It was like the ground has turned gold as far as the eye could see! And the lake– Cyrene pushed me in, once, and I spent the whole day trying to dry out in the sun.

You'd like to see it?

I'm afraid that's not possible. The whole place got swallowed up by the black tide.

I did try to go back, once. I couldn't find it. There's no evidence it ever existed at all.

~

The Flamechase, if it can be called that, continues. He feels restless waiting for Stelle, perhaps more than anyone. The Demigod of Strife should be leading an endless hunt, not waiting for a savior, but there's nothing he can really do about it.

He does chase down the traces of the black tide, where it does exist. He's told that in previous cycles, it was inescapable. He's told that the Deliverer, in his fight against Irontomb, damaged the Ravager enough to almost erase the black tide completely.

Phainon used to compete with him over who could kill more monsters. He wonders if, where he is, he knows he won.

~

Mydei! It's time to go to the baths!

Yes, we get to go a second time! I already booked a timeslot, so you can't say no.

You really can't. I mean it. This isn't a question. We're going.

~

There's still one monster that needs hunting, even with the black tide gone. Lygus has never quite stopped coming after the Chrysos Heirs, even as he prattles on about the heights he'll bring them too.

Unfortunately, it's proven difficult to so much as hold back the damn droid. Mydei, however, has an idea– his soul, split five ways. The aspects of Strife can hold back Lygus without him.

He doesn't really need to be human. The only person he would want to see as one is gone.

~

… If I wasn't the Deliverer?

That's easy. I’d be on the farm, helping my dad.

What about you, mister crown prince? What would you be if you weren't the son of Gorgo?

You don't know? Fair enough. I wasn't exactly creative.

Oh?

I'm not laughing at you. I was thinking that would be nice. I'm sure you'd be good in the fields, too. Even the most tedious work would be fun with you at my side.

~

As his divinity fades, as he feels himself dying, he drags himself to the corner of Castrum Kremnos with the best view of Kephale. He knows the spot intimately though he has never been here before.

Of course I'm worried. I don't know that I have what it takes to reclaim Worldbearing.

“You do,” Mydei mumbles. “Of course you do.”

You're right. Actually– I don't know why I was worried. It's not like you wanted to reclaim Strife, but you make a fine Demigod if I do say so myself.

“I did it for your sake.”

Ah, look at you, King of Castrum Kremnos. So gracious and noble, I hardly recognize you.

The dawn device ebbs. Mydei can feel his soul spitting– it is nearly over. Soon, he'll be reduced to fragments powerful enough to fight Lygus but not to dream of the Deliverer.

“If there's a chance in the next life,” he says, so delirious he can't tell if he's actually spoken aloud, “you should come visit my library.”

It's a date, Mydeimos.
